claim: Tone-elicited freezing was lower after PRF conditioning than fully reinforced fear (FRF) conditioning, despite an equivalent number of tone-shock pairings.
source: Tone-elicited freezing was lower after PRF conditioning than fully reinforced fear (FRF) conditioning, despite an equivalent number of tone-shock pairings.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1C showing statistically significant differences in freezing between PRF and FRF groups.

claim: PRF preferentially activated medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST).
source: PRF preferentially activated medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST).
evidence: The claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data showing higher neuronal activation in these regions in PRF mice, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of BNST-projecting mPFC neurons increased PRF, not FRF, freezing.
source: Chemogenetic inhibition of BNST-projecting mPFC neurons increased PRF, not FRF, freezing.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from chemogenetic manipulation experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Elevated infralimbic cortex (IL) neuronal activity occurs during CS onset and freezing cessation.
source: Multiplexing chemogenetics with in vivo neuronal recordings showed elevated infralimbic cortex (IL) neuronal activity during CS onset and freezing cessation
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo single-unit recording data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: IL neural correlates of CS onset and freezing cessation were abolished by chemogenetic mPFC→BNST inhibition.
source: these neural correlates were abolished by chemogenetic mPFC→BNST inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiplexed chemogenetic and electrophysiology data showing loss of CS-ON and Freeze-OFF neuronal responses in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: mPFC→BNST neurons limit fear to threats with a history of partial association with an aversive stimulus.
source: These data suggest that mPFC→BNST neurons limit fear to threats with a history of partial association with an aversive stimulus, with potential implications for understanding the neural basis of trauma-related disorders.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined chemogenetic and behavioral data showing that inhibition of this pathway increases PRF freezing.

claim: In many cases of psychological trauma, encounters with contexts and stimuli during aversive experience(s) are interleaved with occasions when the same stimuli are experienced without consequence.
source: In many cases of psychological trauma, encounters with contexts and stimuli during aversive experience(s) are interleaved with occasions when the same stimuli are experienced without consequence.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the nature of traumatic experiences.

claim: Most standard rodent assays of fear memory present the subject with a conditioning stimulus (CS) that on each occasion is paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus (US).
source: Most standard rodent assays of fear (i.e., threat) memory, however, present the subject with a conditioning stimulus (CS) that on each occasion is paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus (US) (Fanselow and Poulos, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on fear conditioning methodology.

claim: Partially reinforced CSs can be more difficult to extinguish than fully reinforced CSs.
source: For example, as compared to fully reinforced CSs, partially reinforced CSs can be more difficult to extinguish and produce lesser conditioned responses, due to associative strength accruing to the conditioning context or through the endowment of the CS with inhibitory (CS = no US) properties (Humphreys, 1939; Fitzgerald, 1963; Rawlins et al., 1985; Rescorla, 2007; Tsetsenis et al., 2007; Miguez et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature on partial reinforcement effects.

claim: Partially reinforced CSs produce lesser conditioned responses than fully reinforced CSs.
source: For example, as compared to fully reinforced CSs, partially reinforced CSs can be more difficult to extinguish and produce lesser conditioned responses, due to associative strength accruing to the conditioning context or through the endowment of the CS with inhibitory (CS = no US) properties (Humphreys, 1939; Fitzgerald, 1963; Rawlins et al., 1985; Rescorla, 2007; Tsetsenis et al., 2007; Miguez et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature on partial reinforcement effects.

claim: The mPFC is engaged in experimental situations requiring integration of higher-order cues or disambiguation between conflicting cues to gate a level of response appropriate to the value of outcome.
source: The mPFC is engaged in experimental situations requiring integration of higher-order cues or disambiguation between conflicting cues to gate a level of response appropriate to the value of outcome (Sharpe and Killcross, 2018; Marek et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on mPFC function.

claim: The BNST has been shown to support learning when a stimulus poorly predicts threat.
source: while the BNST has been shown to support learning when a stimulus poorly predicts threat (Lebow and Chen, 2016; Goode et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on BNST function.

claim: There is a particularly dense connection between the IL and the anterior regions of the BNST.
source: These structures are also anatomically connected, with a particularly dense connection between the IL and the anterior regions of the BNST (Hurley et al., 1991; McDonald et al., 1999; Dong et al., 2001; Vertes, 2004; Radley and Sawchenko, 2011; Radley et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2016; Glangetas et al., 2017; Tillman et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: BNST-projecting IL cells are activated by 'unpredictable' threat in a backward conditioning paradigm.
source: Additionally, BNST-projecting IL cells are activated by 'unpredictable' threat in a backward conditioning paradigm (Goode et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on IL-BNST circuit function.

claim: Stimulation of glutamatergic mPFC inputs produces synaptic depression in the BNST.
source: Moreover, stimulation of glutamatergic mPFC inputs produces synaptic depression in the BNST (Glangetas et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior electrophysiology literature.

claim: Freezing increased to a similar extent over the six conditioning trials in the PRF group and over the three conditioning trials in FRF group.
source: Freezing increased to a similar extent over the six conditioning trials in the PRF group and over the three conditioning trials, plus the corresponding three no-trial periods, in FRF group, but did not significantly increase in the CS-only group (analysis of variance [ANOVA] group-effect: F(2,17)=5.74, p=0.0125; trial-effect: F(5,85)=13.49, p<0.0001; interaction: F(5,85)=1.64, p=0.1099).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data during conditioning.

claim: The PRF and FRF groups froze more than CS-only controls during pre-CS baseline and CS presentation on retrieval test.
source: On a retrieval test conducted in a novel context (context B) the following day, the PRF and FRF groups froze more than CS-only controls during pre-CS baseline and CS presentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from retrieval testing shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CS-evoked freezing was lower in the PRF, relative to the FRF, group during retrieval.
source: Notably, however, CS-evoked freezing was lower in the PRF, relative to the FRF, group (ANOVA group-effect: F(2,17)=53.02, p<0.0001; CS-effect: F(1,17)=216.90, p=0.0001; interaction: F(2,17)=25.51, p=0.0001, followed by post-hoc tests: CS-only vs PRF p<0.0001, CS-only vs FRF p<0.0001, PRF vs FRF p=0.0008)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data during retrieval testing.

claim: B6 mice express less freezing in the PRF, as compared to FRF, procedure despite the number of CS–US pairings being equivalent in both conditions.
source: These data show that B6 mice express less freezing in the PRF, as compared to FRF, procedure despite the number of CS–US pairings being equivalent in both conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the behavioral data showing differential freezing despite equivalent shock pairings.

claim: Lower freezing in the PRF procedure in B6 mice is in line with lower freezing in the PRF procedure in a mixed C57BL/6J;CBA/J;129S6/SvEvTac genetic background.
source: These differences are in line with lower freezing in the PRF procedure in a mixed C57BL/6J;CBA/J;129S6/SvEvTac genetic background (Tsetsenis et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature showing similar effects in a different genetic background.

claim: Freezing is equivalent between PRF and FRF groups in outbred CD-1 mice.
source: but, indicating a degree of strain dependency of PRF, differ from data in outbred CD-1 mice, in which freezing is equivalent between PRF and FRF groups (Glover et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature showing different effects in CD-1 mice.

claim: S1 mice exhibit impaired contextual (and cued) fear discrimination.
source: We next reasoned that an inbred strain (S1), which exhibits impaired contextual (and cued) fear discrimination, deficits in limiting fear following extinction and conditioned inhibition, and high fear expression in a different assay for PRF (Camp et al., 2012), might exhibit deficits in the current PRF assay (Camp et al., 2009; Camp et al., 2012; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing the S1 strain phenotype.

claim: S1 mice exhibit deficits in limiting fear following extinction and conditioned inhibition.
source: We next reasoned that an inbred strain (S1), which exhibits impaired contextual (and cued) fear discrimination, deficits in limiting fear following extinction and conditioned inhibition, and high fear expression in a different assay for PRF (Camp et al., 2012), might exhibit deficits in the current PRF assay (Camp et al., 2009; Camp et al., 2012; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing the S1 strain phenotype.

claim: S1 mice exhibit high fear expression in a different assay for PRF.
source: We next reasoned that an inbred strain (S1), which exhibits impaired contextual (and cued) fear discrimination, deficits in limiting fear following extinction and conditioned inhibition, and high fear expression in a different assay for PRF (Camp et al., 2012), might exhibit deficits in the current PRF assay (Camp et al., 2009; Camp et al., 2012; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing the S1 strain phenotype.

claim: PRF B6 mice showed less CS-related freezing than their FRF counterparts during retrieval.
source: On retrieval in context B, PRF B6 mice showed less CS-related freezing than their FRF counterparts, whereas freezing was equivalent in PRF and FRF S1 mice (ANOVA strain-effect: F(1,27)=8.72, p=0.0065; conditioning-type effect: F(1,27)=6.15, p=0.0197; CS-effect: F(1,27) = 524.00, p<0.0001; three-way interaction: F(1,27)=7.03, p=0.0132, followed by post-hoc tests: PRF vs FRF in B6 p=0.0038, PRF vs FRF in S1 p=0.2322)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing B6 and S1 strains.

claim: Freezing was equivalent in PRF and FRF S1 mice during retrieval.
source: On retrieval in context B, PRF B6 mice showed less CS-related freezing than their FRF counterparts, whereas freezing was equivalent in PRF and FRF S1 mice (ANOVA strain-effect: F(1,27)=8.72, p=0.0065; conditioning-type effect: F(1,27)=6.15, p=0.0197; CS-effect: F(1,27) = 524.00, p<0.0001; three-way interaction: F(1,27)=7.03, p=0.0132, followed by post-hoc tests: PRF vs FRF in B6 p=0.0038, PRF vs FRF in S1 p=0.2322)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing B6 and S1 strains.

claim: S1 mice exhibit similar freezing to the PRF and FRF procedures, which aligns with the excessive fear shown by this strain to innocuous stimuli and following extinction.
source: The finding that S1 mice exhibit similar freezing to the PRF and FRF procedures aligns with the excessive fear shown by this strain to innocuous stimuli and following extinction (Camp et al., 2009; Camp et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the current data and supported by citations to prior literature on S1 strain phenotype.

claim: The novelty-suppressed feeding (NSF) test is an assay sensitive to anxiolytics and antidepressants.
source: An earlier study by Glover et al., 2017 found that following PRF conditioning, CD-1 mice had a higher latency to feed, as compared to a FRF group, in the novelty-suppressed feeding (NSF) test, an assay sensitive to anxiolytics and antidepressants (Ramaker and Dulawa, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature characterizing the NSF test.

claim: Following PRF conditioning, CD-1 mice had a higher latency to feed in the NSF test compared to a FRF group.
source: An earlier study by Glover et al., 2017 found that following PRF conditioning, CD-1 mice had a higher latency to feed, as compared to a FRF group, in the novelty-suppressed feeding (NSF) test, an assay sensitive to anxiolytics and antidepressants (Ramaker and Dulawa, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Under high, but not low, illumination, latencies to feed were higher in the PRF and FRF groups than unconditioned controls in the NSF test.
source: Under high, but not low, illumination, latencies to feed were higher in the PRF and FRF groups than unconditioned controls (ANOVA group-effect: F(1,44)=10.93, p=0.0019; illumination-effect: F(1,44)=4.11, p=0.0230; interaction: F(1,44)=2.83, p=0.0699, followed by post hoc tests: PRF vs Con p=0.0004, FRF vs Con p=0.0222)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of NSF behavioral data.

claim: PRF conditioning increases anxiodepressive-like anxiety-like behavior under relatively aversive (high illumination) conditions of approach–avoidance conflict.
source: These data show that PRF conditioning increases anxiodepressive-like anxiety-like behavior under relatively aversive (high illumination) conditions of approach–avoidance conflict.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the NSF behavioral data.

claim: There were a higher number of c-Fos+ cells in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) of FRF mice compared to either PRF mice or CS-only controls.
source: There were a higher number of c-Fos+ cells in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) of FRF mice (ANOVA group-effect: F(2,17)=6.79, p=0.0068, followed by post hoc tests: FRF vs CS-only p=0.0038, FRF vs PRF p=0.0132), as compared to either PRF mice or a set of controls that had received CS-only trials during conditioning.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: c-Fos+ counts in the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT) were higher in the PRF and FRF groups than controls.
source: In the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT), another region implicated in fear (Penzo et al., 2015), c-Fos+ counts were higher in the PRF and FRF groups than controls (ANOVA group-effect: F(2,17)=4.01, p=0.0374, followed by post-hoc tests: CS-only vs PRF p=0.0281, CS-only vs FRF p=0.0145).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data and citation to prior literature on PVT function.

claim: No group differences in c-Fos+ counts were evident in the lateral or medial habenula, or ventral or dorsal hippocampus.
source: No group differences were evident in the lateral or medial habenula, or ventral or dorsal hippocampus (Figure 2A–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claim: There were more c-Fos+ cells in the IL of PRF and FRF mice, relative to CS-only controls.
source: In subregions of the mPFC, however, there were more c-Fos+ cells in the IL (F(2,17)=8.21, p=0.0032, followed by post-hoc tests: CS-only vs PRF p=0.0009, CS-only vs FRF p=0.0411, FRF vs PRF p=0.0420), but not the posterior ACC (F(2,17)=1.01, p=0.3862) of PRF and FRF mice, relative to CS-only controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: c-Fos+ counts in the PL were higher in PRF mice relative to controls and trended higher in the FRF group.
source: Counts in the PL were higher in PRF mice relative to controls and trended higher in the FRF group (F(2,17)=3.60, p=0.0499, followed by post hoc tests: CS-only vs PRF p=0.0196).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Elevated c-Fos activity in the PRF group, relative to the other groups, was evident in the anteroventral BNST (avBNST), not the anterodorsal BNST (adBNST).
source: The same pattern of elevated activity in the PRF group, relative to the other groups, was also evident in the BNST, though specifically in the anteroventral BNST (avBNST) (F(2,17)=19.43, p=0.0001, followed by post hoc tests: CS-only vs PRF p=0.0001, CS-only vs FRF p=0.0294, PRF vs FRF p=0.0005), not the anterodorsal BNST (adBNST) (F(2,14)=1.38, p=0.2831)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Retrieval of a PRF CS, despite being characterized by lower freezing than FRF, associates with a unique pattern of regional brain activation, with preferentially high activation in the IL and PL subregions of the mPFC and the avBNST.
source: These findings show that retrieval of a PRF CS, despite being characterized by lower freezing than FRF, associates with a unique pattern of regional brain activation, with preferentially high activation in the IL and PL subregions of the mPFC and the avBNST.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the c-Fos immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Previous studies in the rat have demonstrated a direct (GABAergic) input from the mPFC to the BNST that is particularly dense between the IL and avBNST.
source: Previous studies in the rat have demonstrated a direct (GABAergic) input from the mPFC to the BNST that is particularly dense between the IL and avBNST (Dong et al., 2001), but also present between the PL and avBNST (Johnson et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies in rats.

claim: A direct input from the mPFC to the BNST is also present between the PL and avBNST in rats.
source: Previous studies in the rat have demonstrated a direct (GABAergic) input from the mPFC to the BNST that is particularly dense between the IL and avBNST (Dong et al., 2001), but also present between the PL and avBNST (Johnson et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies in rats.

claim: mCherry labeling was apparent in BNST neurons, mainly in the ventral areas below the anterior commissure, indicative of monosynaptic input from the mPFC.
source: Indicative of monosynaptic input from the mPFC, mCherry labeling was apparent in BNST neurons, mainly in the ventral areas below the anterior commissure.
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-synaptic tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the rat, PL neurons form close appositions with GABAergic cells in the avBNST that in turn send efferents to the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN).
source: In the rat, PL neurons form close appositions with GABAergic cells in the avBNST that in turn send efferents to the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN), a key mediator of responses to stress and defensive behaviors (Johnson et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies in rats.

claim: The PVN is a key mediator of responses to stress and defensive behaviors.
source: In the rat, PL neurons form close appositions with GABAergic cells in the avBNST that in turn send efferents to the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN), a key mediator of responses to stress and defensive behaviors (Johnson et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PVN function.

claim: mCherry/synaptophysin expression originating from mPFC-innervated BNST neurons was found in the PVN and lateral hypothalamus in mice.
source: Indicating that a similar connection is likely present in mice, inspection of our tissue revealed mCherry/synaptophysin expression originating from mPFC-innervated BNST neurons in the PVN, as well as lateral hypothalamus.
evidence: The claim is supported by trans-synaptic tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Labeling from oxytocin-positive PVN cells was found in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vl/PAG) in mice.
source: To gain initial insight into this question, we infused a Cre-dependent, YFP-fused construct containing either channelrohodpsin2 (ChR2) or synaptophysin into the PVN of oxytocin-Cre mice, to label a major population of (oxytocin-positive) PVN cells. This indicated labeling in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vl/PAG) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by viral tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The vl/PAG is a region known to regulate defensive behaviors including freezing.
source: This indicated labeling in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vl/PAG) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), a region known to regulate defensive behaviors including freezing (Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on vl/PAG function.

claim: There is evidence of input from the mPFC to the BNST in the mouse.
source: Together these data provide evidence of input from the mPFC to the BNST in the mouse, as well as onward connections from the BNST to the PVN and in turn possibly on to the vl/PAG.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the trans-synaptic tracing data.

claim: There are onward connections from the BNST to the PVN in mice.
source: Together these data provide evidence of input from the mPFC to the BNST in the mouse, as well as onward connections from the BNST to the PVN and in turn possibly on to the vl/PAG.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the trans-synaptic tracing data.

claim: There are possibly connections from the PVN to the vl/PAG in mice.
source: Together these data provide evidence of input from the mPFC to the BNST in the mouse, as well as onward connections from the BNST to the PVN and in turn possibly on to the vl/PAG.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the tracing data showing PVN projections to vl/PAG.

claim: PRF engagement of the mPFC and BNST can be viewed in the context of a direct connection between these regions and their downstream access to a broader fear-regulating neural circuitry.
source: Thus, PRF engagement of the mPFC and BNST can be viewed in the context of a direct connection between these regions and their downstream access to a broader fear-regulating neural circuitry.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined c-Fos and tracing data.

claim: CS-related freezing during retrieval was lower in PRF mice than in FRF mice expressing the control virus.
source: Following CNO administration, CS-related freezing during retrieval was lower in PRF mice than in FRF mice expressing the control virus, replicating our earlier data.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from the chemogenetic experiment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was no difference in freezing between PRF and FRF mice expressing hM4Di during retrieval.
source: By contrast, there was no difference in freezing in mice expressing hM4Di (ANOVA conditioning-type effect: F(1,29)=9.35, p=0.0048; virus-group effect: F(1,29)=12.15, p=0.0016; CS: F(1,29)=1331.02, p<0.0001; three-way interaction: F(1,29)=6.58, p=0.0157, followed by post-hoc tests: mCherry PRF vs mCherry FRF p<0.0001, hM4Di PRF vs hM4Di FRF p=0.1425, mCherry PRF vs hM4Di PRF p=0.0013, mCherry PRF vs hM4Di PRF p=0.7951)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from the chemogenetic experiment.

claim: Inhibition of mPFC→BNST neurons increases freezing to a PRF CS.
source: These data show that inhibition of mPFC→BNST neurons increases freezing to a PRF CS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the chemogenetic behavioral data.

claim: Engagement of mPFC→BNST neurons limits the expression of fear to the unreliable, PRF CS.
source: This finding suggests that engagement of these mPFC→BNST neurons limits the expression ofto the unreliable, PRF, though it remains possible that inhibition of these neurons also produces an increase in PRF expression, which may have been masked due to high (ceiling) levels of freezing.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the chemogenetic data, with acknowledgment of alternative interpretations.

claim: A subset of IL neurons were phasically active to CS presentation during fear retrieval.
source: As in our prior studies of FRF in mice (Fitzgerald et al., 2014; Fitzgerald et al., 2015), a subset of IL neurons were phasically active to CS presentation during fear retrieval.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo single-unit recording data and citations to prior studies.

claim: A subset of IL neurons displayed phasic activity during the cessation, but not onset, of freezing during fear retrieval.
source: Intriguingly, we also found a subset of IL neurons that displayed phasic activity during the cessation, but not onset, of freezing during fear retrieval, echoing recordings in rats that uncovered movement-related activity in IL units (Halladay and Blair, 2015; Halladay and Blair, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo single-unit recording data and citations to prior studies in rats.

claim: Inhibition of BNST-projecting mPFC neurons during fear retrieval essentially abolished the CS- and Freeze-OFF-associated neuronal activity in IL neurons.
source: Inhibition of BNST-projecting mPFC neurons during fear retrieval essentially abolished the CS- and Freeze-OFF-associated neuronal activity in IL neurons and, in parallel, increased freezing in the PRF group.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiplexed chemogenetic and electrophysiology data.

claim: Inhibition of BNST-projecting mPFC neurons during fear retrieval increased freezing in the PRF group.
source: Inhibition of BNST-projecting mPFC neurons during fear retrieval essentially abolished the CS- and Freeze-OFF-associated neuronal activity in IL neurons and, in parallel, increased freezing in the PRF group.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiplexed chemogenetic and electrophysiology data.

claim: CS-ON units showed a significant change in neuronal activity in response to the CS.
source: Overall, CS-ON units showed a significant change in neuronal activity in response to the CS (baseline: 0.15 ± 0.35, post-CS: 1.43 ± 0.55, paired t-test: t(10)=6.51, p<0.0001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of single-unit recording data.

claim: There was a higher proportion of CS-ON units in the mCherry groups than in hM4Di groups for PRF mice.
source: However, when the percentage of CS-ON units was calculated and compared across the conditioning and virus groups, this revealed a higher proportion of CS-ON units in the mCherry groups than in hM4Di groups for PRF mice (Fisher's exact test: p=0.0122), but no differences between virus groups in the FRF mice (Fisher's exact test: p=0.6090), and no difference between PRF and FRF groups, irrespective of virus group (Fisher's exact test in mCherry: p=0.2510; in hM4Di: p=1.000)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of single-unit recording data.

claim: Freeze-ON units displayed a significant change in baseline-normalized activity.
source: These units, classified as Freeze-ON and Freeze-OFF, respectively, showed a significant change in baseline-normalized activity (Freeze-ON baseline: −0.81 ± 0.47, post-event: −2.12 ± 0.52, paired t-test: t(10)=4.60, p=0.0010, Freeze-OFF baseline: 0.73 ± 0.43, post-event: 1.67 ± 0.40, paired t-test: t(12)=8.54, p<0.0001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of single-unit recording data.

claim: Freeze-OFF units showed a significant change in baseline-normalized activity.
source: These units, classified as Freeze-ON and Freeze-OFF, respectively, showed a significant change in baseline-normalized activity (Freeze-ON baseline: −0.81 ± 0.47, post-event: −2.12 ± 0.52, paired t-test: t(10)=4.60, p=0.0010, Freeze-OFF baseline: 0.73 ± 0.43, post-event: 1.67 ± 0.40, paired t-test: t(12)=8.54, p<0.0001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of single-unit recording data.

claim: There was a higher percentage of Freeze-OFF units in the mCherry PRF group than in the hM4Di PRF group.
source: When the percentage of these cell types were compared across groups, there was a higher percentage of Freeze-OFF units in the mCherry PRF group than in the hM4Di PRF group (Fisher's exact test: p=0.0024), whereas there was no group difference in FRF mice (Fisher's exact test: p=1.000) and no difference between PRF and FRF groups in either the mCherry (Fisher's exact test: p=0.4600) or hM4Di (Fisher's exact test: p=0.0590) virus conditions
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of single-unit recording data.

claim: There was no difference between the mCherry and hM4Di groups in the proportion of Freeze-ON units, irrespective of whether mice had undergone PRF or FRF.
source: Conversely, there was no difference between the mCherry and hM4Di groups in the proportion of Freeze-ON units, irrespective of whether mice had undergone PRF or FRF.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of single-unit recording data.

claim: The current findings align with and extend prior work implicating the mPFC and BNST in various situations in which there is ambiguity and uncertainty about a threat.
source: The current findings align with and extend prior work implicating the mPFC and BNST in various situations in which there is ambiguity and uncertainty about a threat.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the current data in the context of prior literature.

claim: The mPFC is engaged in settings that require integration of higher-order cues to gate learned responses.
source: For example, the mPFC is engaged in settings that require integration of higher-order cues to gate learned responses (Halladay and Blair, 2015; Halladay and Blair, 2017; Sharpe and Killcross, 2018; Marek et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on mPFC function.

claim: The mPFC is engaged where there is conflict between excitatory and inhibitory CS associations, for instance in fear extinction.
source: or where there is conflict between excitatory and inhibitory CS associations, for instance in fear extinction (Milad and Quirk, 2012; Bloodgood et al., 2018; Lay et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on mPFC function in extinction.

claim: The mPFC is engaged in fear discrimination.
source: fear discrimination (Grosso et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on mPFC function.

claim: The mPFC is engaged in threat/safety conditioning.
source: threat/safety conditioning (Sangha et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on mPFC function.

claim: The mPFC is engaged in punished reward-seeking.
source: and punished reward-seeking (Burgos-Robles et al., 2017; Halladay et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on mPFC function.

claim: The BNST supports learning in the absence of the BLA.
source: The BNST, meanwhile, supports learning in the absence of the BLA (Poulos et al., 2010; Zimmerman and Maren, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on BNST function.

claim: The BNST supports learning when a stimulus poorly predicts threat because it is distal (e.g., predator odor).
source: and when a stimulus poorly predicts threat (Lebow and Chen, 2016; Goode et al., 2019; Bjorni et al., 2020), either because it is distal (e.g., predator odor; Fendt et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2012; Breitfeld et al., 2015; Verma et al., 2018; Goode et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on BNST function.

claim: The BNST supports learning when a stimulus poorly predicts threat because it is diffuse (e.g., contextual).
source: diffuse (e.g., contextual; Sullivan et al., 2004; Kalin et al., 2005; Duvarci et al., 2009; Davis et al., 2010; Luyten et al., 2012; Jennings et al., 2013; c.f. Haufler et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on BNST function.

claim: The BNST supports learning when a stimulus poorly predicts threat because it is temporally ambiguous (e.g., random or sustained) with respect to the US.
source: or temporally ambiguous (e.g., random or sustained; Waddell et al., 2006; Walker et al., 2009; Hammack et al., 2015; Daldrup et al., 2016; Goode and Maren, 2017; Lange et al., 2017) with respect to the US.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on BNST function.

claim: The known functions of the mPFC and BNST make these structures well placed to mediate fear under conditions of partial reinforcement where the CS is experienced both with and without the US.
source: These known functions of the mPFC and BNST make these structures well placed to mediate fear under conditions of partial reinforcement where the CS is experienced both with and without the US.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the current data in the context of prior literature on mPFC and BNST function.

claim: The mPFC and BNST form a discrete neural circuit that serves to limit the expression of partially reinforced fear.
source: As we show here, the mPFC and BNST form a discrete neural circuit, through a direct anatomical connection, that serves to limit the expression of partially reinforced fear.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined anatomical and functional data.

claim: IL neurons projecting to the avBNST are activated (measured by c-Fos) by a measure of unpredictable threat (backward conditioning), in which US presentation precedes the CS.
source: This observation is reminiscent of a recent study showing that IL neurons projecting to the avBNST are activated (measured by c-Fos) by a measure of unpredictable threat (backward conditioning), in which US presentation precedes the CS (Goode and Maren, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There is convergent evidence supporting a key role for the mPFC→BNST circuit in mediating fear across various measures of threat uncertainty, ambiguity, and unpredictability.
source: In conjunction with the current data, there is convergent evidence supporting a key role for the mPFC→BNST circuit in mediating fear across various measures of threat uncertainty, ambiguity, and unpredictability.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the current data in the context of prior literature.

claim: When discrete cues are relatively poor predictors of danger, other environmental stimuli, such as context, may modulate the expression of fear in a manner that recruits the mPFC to exert top-down control over the BNST.
source: One possibility is that when discrete cues are relatively poor predictors of danger, other environmental stimuli, such as context, modulate the expression of fear in a manner that recruits the mPFC to exert top-down control over the BNST.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for mPFC-BNST function in PRF.

claim: The mPFC is posited to subserve higher-order modulation of conditioned responding.
source: In support of this possibility, the mPFC is posited to subserve higher-order modulation of conditioned responding (Sharpe and Killcross, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on mPFC function.

claim: Lesions of either the PL or IL impaired one measure of occasion setting in rats.
source: indeed, a recent study in rats found that lesions of either the PL or IL impaired one measure of such modulation known as occasion setting (Roughley and Killcross, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CS-alone presentations during conditioning may imbue the CS with inhibitory properties that are gated by mPFC→BNST neurons during retrieval.
source: Another possible explanation for the increase in PRF caused by mPFC→BNST inhibition is that CS-alone presentations during conditioning imbues the CS with inhibitory properties that are gated by mPFC→BNST neurons during retrieval.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing an alternative mechanism for mPFC-BNST function in PRF.

claim: Learned inhibition is a function attributed to the mPFC and in particular the IL.
source: Learned inhibition is a function attributed to the mPFC and in particular the IL.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about IL function.

claim: Pharmacological, optogenetic, and chemogenetic inhibition of the IL impairs the formation and/or retrieval of fear extinction memories.
source: For example, pharmacological, optogenetic, and chemogenetic inhibition of the IL impairs the formation and/or retrieval of fear extinction memories (Laurent and Westbrook, 2009; Bukalo et al., 2015; Do-Monte et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Lay et al., 2020; Bukalo et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on IL function in extinction.

claim: IL inhibition impairs the expression of learned safety acquired through explicit CS–US unpairing.
source: and the expression of learned safety acquired through explicit CS–US unpairing (Sangha et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on IL function in safety learning.

claim: Presentation of a safety signal during inescapable stress decreases activity (c-Fos) in a lateral area of BNST encompassing avBNST.
source: Conversely, presentation of a safety signal during inescapable stress decreases activity (c-Fos) in a lateral area of BNST encompassing avBNST (Christianson et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on BNST function.

claim: Lesioning a lateral area of BNST reduces inappropriate fear to a non-reinforced CS in rats with high-trait anxiety.
source: Furthermore, lesioning this area reduces inappropriate fear to a non-reinforced CS in rats with high-trait anxiety (Duvarci et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on BNST function.

claim: A growing number of lesion and functional neuroimaging studies in non-human primates and humans have implicated the BNST in the processing of uncertain threat.
source: Indeed, a growing number of lesion and functional neuroimaging studies in non-human primates and humans have implicated the BNST in the processing of uncertain threat (see Goode et al., 2019; Miles and Maren, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review literature on BNST function in uncertain threat.

claim: Inhibitory properties of the partially reinforced CS could be signaled by the IL downstream to the BNST, thereby limiting the expression of CS-induced fear to a level appropriate to its partial reinforcement history.
source: Together, these findings suggest that inhibitory properties of the partially reinforced CS could be signaled by the IL downstream to the BNST, thereby limiting the expression of CS-induced fear to a level appropriate to its partial reinforcement history.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on inference from prior literature and current data.

claim: The small size and ventral location of the IL and avBNST meant that viral transfection encompassed parts of the PL and adBNST.
source: It is important to note in this regard that while we targeted our virus infusions to the IL and avBNST – based on prior evidence of a dense anatomical connection between these subregions – the small size and ventral location of these areas meant that viral transfection encompassed parts of the PL and adBNST.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a technical limitation of the viral targeting approach.

claim: The adBNST is engaged by challenges that produce negative affect.
source: The adBNST is engaged by challenges that produce negative affect (Centanni et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on adBNST function.

claim: The adBNST undergoes plastic changes in response to chronic stress.
source: undergoes plastic changes in response to chronic stress (Conrad et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on adBNST plasticity.

claim: The adBNST is a target of dorsal raphe, BLA, and central amygdala neurons that sustain fear responses to predictable and unpredictable threats.
source: and, of particular relevance here, is a target of dorsal raphe (Marcinkiewcz et al., 2016), BLA (Lange et al., 2017), and central amygdala (Asok et al., 2018) neurons that sustain fear responses to predictable and unpredictable threats.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on adBNST connectivity and function.

claim: The adBNST is less densely innervated by the mPFC than the avBNST.
source: As such, although the adBNST is a less densely innervated by the mPFC (Hurley et al., 1991; McDonald et al., 1999; Dong et al., 2001; Vertes, 2004; Radley and Sawchenko, 2011; Radley et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2016; Glangetas et al., 2017; Tillman et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical literature.

claim: Current and prior c-Fos data do not indicate adBNST activation with uncertain threat.
source: and current as well as prior (Goode et al., 2019) c-Fos data do not indicate adBNST activation with uncertain threat
evidence: The claim is supported by the current c-Fos data and citation to prior literature.

claim: It would be premature to exclude a contribution of the adBNST to PRF.
source: it would be premature to exclude a contribution of this area to PRF.
evidence: The claim is speculative, acknowledging uncertainty about the role of adBNST.

claim: The possible contribution of BNST-targeting PL neurons to PRF should not be discounted.
source: The possible contribution of BNST-targeting PL neurons to PRF also should not be discounted.
evidence: The claim is speculative, acknowledging uncertainty about the role of PL inputs.

claim: The PL has been ascribed a role in promoting FRF via its outputs to the BLA.
source: While the PL has been ascribed a role in promoting FRF via its outputs to the BLA (Pape and Pare, 2010; Dias et al., 2013; Bukalo et al., 2014; Tovote et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PL function.

claim: Optogenetically silencing PL inputs to the avBNST increased immobility and associated stress hormone responses in the rat shock-probe burying and tail suspension tests.
source: recent work found that optogenetically silencing PL inputs to the avBNST increased immobility and associated stress hormone responses in the rat shock-probe burying and tail suspension tests (Johnson et al., 2019; see also Radley et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PL-BNST circuit function.

claim: The effects of silencing PL inputs to the avBNST suggest a role for PL inputs in attenuating negative affect.
source: These effects suggest a role for PL inputs in attenuating negative affect and as such are broadly congruent and potentially explanatory of the current data, despite important differences in methodology.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from prior literature in the context of the current findings.

claim: A subset of IL neurons were phasically active to CS presentation during fear retrieval in the current study, as in prior studies of FRF in mice.
source: In the current study, we found neuronal correlates of PRF, specifically within the IL. As in our prior studies of FRF in mice (Fitzgerald et al., 2014; Fitzgerald et al., 2015), a subset of IL neurons were phasically active to CS presentation during fear retrieval.
evidence: The claim is supported by the current single-unit recording data and citations to prior studies.

claim: Recordings in rats uncovered movement-related activity in IL units.
source: Intriguingly, we also found a subset of IL neurons that displayed phasic activity during the cessation, but not onset, of freezing during fear retrieval, echoing recordings in rats that uncovered movement-related activity in IL units (Halladay and Blair, 2015; Halladay and Blair, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on IL unit activity in rats.

claim: The ability of mPFC→BNST inhibition to ablate CS- and Freeze-OFF-associated neuronal correlates could have arisen from the chemogenetic inhibition of BNST-projecting IL neurons, resulting in a loss-of-function in this pathway and a selective increase in PRF mice.
source: The ability of mPFC→BNST inhibition to ablate these neuronal correlates could have arisen from the chemogenetic inhibition of BNST-projecting IL neurons, resulting in a loss-of-function in this pathway and a selective increase in PRF mice.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the multiplexed chemogenetic and electrophysiology data.

claim: Inhibition-induced increases in freezing in FRF mice may have been masked by a performance 'ceiling' in the FRF control group.
source: Two caveats to this interpretation are that, firstly, inhibition-induced increases in freezing in FRF mice may have been masked by a performance 'ceiling' in the FRF control group
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing an alternative interpretation of the data.

claim: hM4Di expression in the recording experiment was not restricted to BNST-projections within the IL, and also encompassed neurons in the PL.
source: and, secondly, hM4Di expression in our recording experiment was not restricted to BNST-projections within the IL, and also encompassed neurons in the PL.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a technical limitation of the viral targeting approach in the recording experiment.

claim: Using trans-synaptic tracing, there is evidence of a disynaptic mPFC→BNST→PVN circuit in mice, as has been reported in rats.
source: With regard to the broader neural circuitry in which the mPFC→BNST circuit operates to mediate PRF, using trans-synaptic tracing, we found evidence of a disynaptic mPFC→BNST→PVN circuit in mice, as has been reported in rats (Radley and Sawchenko, 2011; Johnson et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by the current tracing data and citations to prior anatomical studies in rats.

claim: The PVN contains a high density of cells expressing peptide hormones implicated in stress and fear, notably corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH) and oxytocin.
source: The PVN contains a high density of cells expressing peptide hormones implicated in stress and fear, notably corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH) and oxytocin (Herman and Tasker, 2016; Triana-Del Río et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PVN neurochemistry.

claim: CRH-expressing neurons in the PVN receive input from the BNST.
source: Though CRH-expressing neurons in the PVN receive input from the BNST (Colmers and Bains, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior literature on BNST-PVN connectivity.

claim: It is unclear whether oxytocin-producing cells in the PVN receive input from the BNST.
source: it is unclear whether oxytocin-producing cells do so.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a gap in knowledge about BNST-PVN connectivity.

claim: Mouse PVN oxytocinergic neurons strongly innervate the freezing-regulating vl/PAG.
source: Interesting nonetheless, we found that mouse PVN oxytocinergic neurons strongly innervate the freezing-regulating vl/PAG, replicating earlier work in cats and naked mole rats (Holstege, 1987; Rosen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by the current tracing data and citations to prior anatomical studies in other species.

claim: The vl/PAG receives input from a population of avBNST neurons that is, in turn, innervated by the PL.
source: Given the vl/PAG also receives input from a population of avBNST neurons that is, in turn, innervated by the PL (Johnson et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical literature.

claim: In addition to directly innervating the PVN, mPFC→avBNST neurons may also have both direct and indirect (via the PVN) access to the vl/PAG.
source: these tracing results suggest that in addition to directly innervating the PVN, mPFC→avBNST neurons may also have both direct and indirect (via the PVN) access to the vl/PAG.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the current and prior tracing data.

claim: The mPFC→BNST circuit is positioned to modulate multiple behavioral and neuroendocrine responses to PRF.
source: This positions the circuit to modulate multiple behavioral and neuroendocrine responses to PRF.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the anatomical connectivity data.

claim: B6 mice expressed lower fear to a CS that is partially, rather than fully, reinforced with footshock.
source: In summary, the current study found that B6 mice expressed lower fear to a CS that is partially, rather than fully, reinforced with footshock.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main behavioral finding of the study.

claim: Lower PRF expression was not apparent in a mouse strain (S1) deficient in fear discrimination and learned inhibition.
source: Lower PRF expression was not apparent in a mouse strain (S1) deficient in fear discrimination and learned inhibition.
evidence: The claim summarizes the strain comparison finding.

claim: c-Fos mapping revealed PRF preferentially recruited the mPFC and BNST.
source: Furthermore, c-Fos mapping revealed PRF preferentially recruited the mPFC and BNST
evidence: The claim summarizes the c-Fos mapping findings.

claim: Neuronal tracing showed direct neuronal projections from mPFC to the BNST, with downstream connections to stress- and fear-mediating regions.
source: and neuronal tracing showed direct neuronal projections from mPFC to the BNST, with downstream connections to stress- and fear-mediating regions.
evidence: The claim summarizes the anatomical tracing findings.

claim: Inhibiting the mPFC→BNST pathway increased PRF and abolished neuronal correlates of CS presentation and freezing cessation in the IL.
source: Demonstrating the causal importance of the mPFC→BNST neurons, inhibiting this pathway increased PRF and abolished neuronal correlates of CS presentation and freezing cessation in the IL.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings from the chemogenetic and electrophysiology experiments.

claim: These findings provide novel insight into the neural substrates of PRF, with potential translational relevance to anxiety and trauma- and stressor-related disorders in which threats are typically ambiguous and unpredictable.
source: Collectively, these findings provide novel insight into the neural substrates of PRF, with potential translational relevance to anxiety and trauma- and stressor-related disorders in which threats are typically ambiguous and unpredictable.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the overall findings and their potential clinical implications.
